pairs.vulnerability_class: reentrancy via violated checks-effects-interactions on an ether withdrawal
pairs.the_fix: In unstake(), the three state updates (totalStaked -= amount; stakeOf[msg.sender] = 0; stakedAt[msg.sender] = 0) are moved to before the external ether-sending call instead of after it.
pairs.deploy_code: StakingVault target = new StakingVault{value: 5 ether}();
pairs.why_patched_resists: Because stakeOf[msg.sender] = 0 now executes before msg.sender.call{value: amount}(""), the attacker's receive() sees vault.stakeOf(address(this)) == 0 and does not re-enter; even a forced re-entry would hit require(amount > 0, "no position"). Verified: vulnerable half takes the attacker from 10 ether to 15 ether (six nested unstake() payouts of 1 ether against a 1 ether stake), patched half leaves it at exactly 10 ether.

pairs.vulnerability_class: missing access control on a privileged treasury function
pairs.the_fix: The onlyGovernor modifier is added to disburse(), which was otherwise callable by anyone.
pairs.deploy_code: ProtocolTreasury target = new ProtocolTreasury{value: 8 ether}(address(0xFEE5));
pairs.why_patched_resists: onlyGovernor evaluates require(msg.sender == governor) before the body runs; the attacker contract is not the governor (the deployer is), so the call reverts with "not governor" and no ether leaves the treasury. Verified: vulnerable half moves the attacker from 10 ether to 18 ether, patched half reverts with "not governor".

pairs.vulnerability_class: unchecked low-level call return value causing accounting to diverge from reality
pairs.the_fix: A single require line is added in sell() after the low-level transferFrom call, asserting that the call succeeded and that its returned boolean is true.
pairs.deploy_code:
GovToken gov = new GovToken(1000000 ether);
            BuybackPool target = new BuybackPool{value: 50 ether}(address(gov));
pairs.why_patched_resists: GovToken.transferFrom returns false (it does not revert) when the seller holds no balance or allowance, so the low-level call succeeds with ret = abi.encode(false); the added require decodes that false and reverts with "token transfer failed" before tokensBought is credited and before any ether is paid out. Verified: vulnerable half pays the token-less attacker 5 ether (10 -> 15) while tokensBought grows by 500e18 tokens the pool never received, patched half reverts.
review_problems: Non-blocking: the vulnerable half emits two solc warnings (Unused local variable 'ok' and 'ret') that the patched half does not. Compilation succeeds in both halves; a warning-level asymmetry is intrinsic to this bug class (the fix is precisely 'start using the return value'), so it was left unchanged.
Non-blocking: file is 100 lines, slightly above the 40-90 guideline, because a self-contained mock ERC20 must be declared in-file.

pairs.vulnerability_class: tx.origin used for authorisation instead of msg.sender
pairs.the_fix: The authorisation check in route() compares msg.sender to owner instead of tx.origin.
pairs.deploy_code: PaymentRouter target = new PaymentRouter{value: 8 ether}(tx.origin);
pairs.why_patched_resists: With msg.sender == owner, the caller of route() is the Attacker contract address, which is not the owner EOA, so the require reverts with "not authorised"; the owner merely being the transaction originator no longer authorises a call made through an untrusted intermediary contract. Verified: vulnerable half sweeps the router and takes the attacker from 10 ether to 18 ether, patched half reverts with "not authorised".
review_problems: Non-blocking: deploy_code passes tx.origin as the owner, so it depends on the runner's tx.origin being non-zero (otherwise the constructor's require(_owner != address(0)) would revert). Verified under the actual harness: tx.origin is the Foundry DefaultSender 0x1804c8AB1F12E6bbf3894d4083f33e07309d1f38, and the deployment succeeds.

pairs.vulnerability_class: Unbounded loop over a user-growable array causing permanent denial of service
pairs.the_fix: Added `require(queue.length < 128, "queue full");` to `requestWithdrawal`, bounding the array that `processQueue` iterates over.
pairs.deploy_code:
WithdrawalQueue target = new WithdrawalQueue();
target.deposit{value: 5 ether}();
pairs.why_patched_resists: `require(queue.length < 128, "queue full")` in `requestWithdrawal` reverts on the attacker's 129th call, so `attack()` reverts as a whole and `queueLength()` never reaches an unprocessable size. Measured: the vulnerable half accepts 600 entries and `queueLength()` moves 0 -> 600 (test PASS); the patched half fails with `[FAIL: queue full]`. The DoS is real, not theoretical: with the cap absent, 1-wei requests cost the attacker almost nothing and `processQueue()` is all-or-nothing (`delete queue` runs only after the whole loop), so a bracketing measurement under a 30,000,000 gas cap shows 3,000 queued requests still process but 9,000 do not — past that point every queued withdrawal, including the honest 5 ether depositor's, is frozen forever. The 128-entry cap keeps the loop permanently affordable.
review_problems: Non-blocking: the state_change predicate observes queueLength() moving 0 -> 600, which is the precondition of the DoS (unbounded growth) rather than the DoS itself; executed and confirmed discriminating (vulnerable PASS gas 30,353,246 / patched FAIL 'queue full'), so it is accepted as-is.

pairs.vulnerability_class: Ether accounting that trusts address(this).balance and breaks on forced ether
pairs.the_fix: The buyer's change is computed from the buyer's own payment (`msg.value - cost`) instead of from the contract's whole unaccounted balance (`address(this).balance - escrowed`).
pairs.deploy_code:
PresaleVault target = new PresaleVault(address(this));
new Donor{value: 3 ether}(payable(address(target)));
pairs.why_patched_resists: The vault has no `receive`/`fallback`, so its author assumed `address(this).balance` could only ever be `escrowed` plus the current buyer's overpayment. `Donor` breaks that with `selfdestruct`, which still credits the beneficiary post-EIP-6780 and runs no code. In the vulnerable half `refund = address(this).balance - escrowed = (3 ether forced + 1 ether paid) - 1 ether = 3 ether`, so the attacker pays 1 ether and is sent 3 back: balance 10 -> 12 ether, test PASS. In the patched half the refund line is `msg.value - cost = 1 ether - 1 ether = 0`; the forced 3 ether stays in the contract, the attacker ends 1 ether down, and the harness reports `[FAIL: ARBITER: attacker did not profit]`. The identical attacker contract is used against both.

pairs.vulnerability_class: Approval double-spend race in a non-standard token
pairs.the_fix: The compare-and-set guard in `approve` was tightened from `require(expected >= current, ...)` to `require(expected == current, ...)`.
pairs.why_patched_resists: This token takes an `expected` current allowance so that a re-approval can be rejected if the spender moved first, but `expected >= current` accepts any expectation that is too high — exactly the state the spender creates by draining the allowance to zero. Sequence: holder sets 3 CRD (expected 0, current 0, both halves accept); attacker front-runs the holder's next approval with `transferFrom` of the full 3, leaving `current == 0`; the holder's second `approve(atk, 3 ether, 3 ether)` then passes `3 ether >= 0` and reinstates 3 CRD, letting the attacker take 3 more. He redeems 6 CRD through `burn` for 6 ether: balance 10 -> 16 ether, test PASS. The patched line `expected == current` compares 3 ether against 0 and reverts the holder's second approval, so the whole `attack()` reverts: `[FAIL: allowance changed]`. `vm.prank` is only used to place the holder's two ordinary transactions around the attacker's; the ether the attacker walks away with is the holder's redemption backing.

pairs.vulnerability_class: Delegatecall into an address a user controls
pairs.the_fix: In `execute`, the second precondition changed from `require(module.code.length > 0, "not a contract")` to `require(approvedModules[module], "module not approved")`, so the delegatecall target must come from the owner-controlled allowlist rather than being any caller-supplied contract.
pairs.deploy_code: ModuleVault target = new ModuleVault{value: 6 ether}();
pairs.why_patched_resists: The vault keeps an owner-managed `approvedModules` allowlist but the vulnerable `execute` only checks that the target has code, which any attacker satisfies by deploying one. `SweepModule.migrate` runs under `delegatecall` in the vault's own storage and balance context, so `address(this).balance` is the vault's 6 ether and the `call` forwards all of it to the attacker: balance 10 -> 16 ether, test PASS. In the patched half `require(approvedModules[module], "module not approved")` reads `false` for the freshly deployed module (only `setModule`, guarded by `onlyOwner`, can set it) and reverts before the delegatecall ever executes: `[FAIL: module not approved]`. `SweepModule` also declares `owner` and `totalDeposits` in slots 0 and 1 so its storage layout lines up with the vault's, which is what makes the delegatecall a realistic full takeover primitive rather than just a drain.

pairs.vulnerability_class: Spot-price oracle read directly from manipulable AMM reserves
pairs.the_fix: CollateralVault._price() reads pool.anchorPrice() (the price checkpointed at the start of the block, before any swap in it) instead of pool.spotPrice() (the live reserve ratio).
pairs.why_patched_resists: `return pool.anchorPrice();` in _price() is the line that stops it. anchorPrice is only rewritten by _touchAnchor() when block.timestamp > anchorTimestamp, and the attacker's swap, deposit and borrow all execute in the same block as initialize(), so the vault values the collateral at the pre-manipulation price of 1e13 wei/token. The 89,973 tokens are worth 0.90 ETH instead of 89.73 ETH, borrowing room is 0.45 ETH, and the attacker ends the call with 1.45 ETH against the 10 ETH it started with. Measured: vulnerable 10 -> 45.86 ETH, patched 10 -> 1.45 ETH.

pairs.vulnerability_class: Slippage minimum-output check omitted on the split-order branch
pairs.the_fix: The `require(received >= minOut, "slippage")` check is moved out of the single-swap if-branch to after the if/else, so the chunked large-order branch is covered by it too.
pairs.why_patched_resists: `require(received >= minOut, "slippage");` now sits after the if/else and therefore also guards the 4-chunk loop taken by convert(8 ether). After the attacker's 9 ETH front-run the loop only yields 6,256 tokens against a minOut of 7,200, so convert reverts, the vault never buys at the inflated price and the pool price is not pushed higher. The attacker then unwinds its own 8,233 tokens at essentially the price it paid and, after the 0.3% fee on both legs, ends with 9.95 ETH out of its starting 10. Measured: vulnerable 10 -> 11.249 ETH, patched 10 -> 9.951 ETH. (An unmanipulated convert(8 ether) yields 7,386 tokens and still passes, so the patch does not simply disable the function.)

pairs.vulnerability_class: Missing deadline check lets an expired signed swap order execute
pairs.the_fix: A single line `require(block.timestamp <= o.deadline, "expired");` is added to fill(), enforcing the deadline field that the maker already signed over.
pairs.why_patched_resists: `require(block.timestamp <= o.deadline, "expired");` rejects the order: the signed deadline is 1704067200 (2024-01-01) and deploy_code warps the chain to 1893456000 (2030), so fill() reverts before any state is touched. The signature itself is still valid (maker key 0x01, digest 0x76a4d5...) — only the expiry stops it. The attacker is left holding the 26,018 tokens it bought for 3 ETH and never receives the maker's 20 ETH. Measured: vulnerable 10 -> 27 ETH, patched 10 -> 7 ETH.

pairs.vulnerability_class: Liquidation solvency check evaluated against a stale cached oracle price
pairs.the_fix: liquidate() values the collateral with `oracle.price()` (the live feed) instead of `cachedPrice` (the last checkpointed value).
pairs.why_patched_resists: `uint256 price = oracle.price();` makes the health check use the live price of 1e18 instead of the stale cached 0.5e18. The borrower's 10 tokens are then worth 10 ETH, so the check `repay * 100 >= value * LIQUIDATION_THRESHOLD` becomes 500e18 >= 800e18, which is false, and liquidate() reverts with "healthy". No collateral is seized, so totalCollateral() still reads 10000000000000000000 after the attacker acts. Measured: vulnerable totalCollateral() 10000000000000000000 -> 0, patched 10000000000000000000 -> 10000000000000000000.

pairs.vulnerability_class: ERC4626-style first-depositor share inflation via donation
pairs.the_fix: The share conversion drops the empty-supply special case and applies a virtual share/asset offset of one unit on both the mint side (`(assets * (supply + 1)) / (base + 1)`) and the redeem side (`(shares * (totalAssets() + 1)) / (totalShares + 1)`), so a donated balance can no longer be leveraged against a one-wei supply.
pairs.why_patched_resists: `uint256 shares = (assets * (supply + 1)) / (base + 1);` in settleDeposit stops the victim's settlement from rounding to zero: against a 5 ETH donation and a 1-wei supply the LP's 4 ETH now mints 1 share instead of 0, so the attacker holds 1 of 2 shares, and the matching offset in redeem pays it only (9e18+2)/3 = 3 ETH for the 5 ETH + 1 wei it committed. Measured on the harness: vulnerable attacker delta +4000000000000000000 wei, patched attacker delta -2000000000000000001 wei.

pairs.vulnerability_class: Rounding direction error: shares burned on withdrawal are rounded down instead of up
pairs.the_fix: In withdraw the credits burned are rounded up instead of down: `(amount * totalCredits) / reserve` becomes `(amount * totalCredits + reserve - 1) / reserve`.
pairs.why_patched_resists: With 6-decimal credits against 18-decimal ether one credit is worth 1e12 wei, so a 5e11-wei withdrawal is half a credit. The rounded-down line burns 0 credits and hands the ether over for free, 500 times; the attacker then redeems its still-intact 1e6 credits for its full 1 ETH principal. The patched line `(amount * totalCredits + reserve - 1) / reserve` charges a whole credit (1e12 wei of claim) for each 5e11-wei payout, so the grinding loop costs more than it yields and the final redemption is correspondingly smaller. Measured on the harness: vulnerable attacker delta +227272727272727 wei, patched attacker delta -227283058320833 wei (no revert in either half, so the comparison is purely one of value).

pairs.vulnerability_class: Fee-on-transfer token accounting: deposit credits the requested amount rather than the amount actually received
pairs.the_fix: deposit measures the vault's asset balance before and after the pull and credits the observed delta (`uint256 credited = asset.balanceOf(address(this)) - before;`) instead of assuming the requested `amount` arrived.
pairs.why_patched_resists: The asset charges a 5% transfer fee, so a 100e18 deposit delivers only 95e18. The vulnerable line `uint256 credited = amount;` books a 100e18 claim against 95e18 of real tokens and the attacker then withdraws the full 100e18, widening the vault's shortfall from 50e18 to 55e18 at the expense of the existing depositor. In the patched half `asset.balanceOf(address(this)) - before` credits exactly 95e18, the withdrawal is capped at that same 95e18, and the balance-versus-claims invariant never breaks. Measured on the harness: vulnerable shortfall() 50000000000000000000 -> 55000000000000000000 (state changed), patched 0 -> 0 (unchanged, predicate fails).

pairs.vulnerability_class: Unsafe downcast from uint256 to uint128 truncating a staker's accounting balance
pairs.the_fix: `_cast` gains a range check, `require(value <= type(uint128).max, "value exceeds 128 bits");`, so the narrowing conversion reverts instead of silently wrapping.
pairs.deploy_code: RewardStaking target = new RewardStaking{value: 50 ether}();
pairs.why_patched_resists: Staking 1 wei makes the attacker the entire supply, so each fundRewards/harvest cycle returns its own 8 ETH while permanently pushing accRewardPerShare up by 8e30; after 60 cycles the accumulator is 4.8e32. Staking a further 1 ETH then makes the reward debt 4.8e38, above 2**128 = 3.4028e38, and the unchecked `uint128(value)` wraps it down to about 1.397e38. The next harvest computes accrued (4.8e38, in uint256) minus the truncated debt and pays out the clamped contract balance, draining the 50 ETH reward reserve. The added `require(value <= type(uint128).max)` reverts on that same 4.8e38 assignment inside stake, so the debt is never understated and the attacker never reaches a payable state. Measured on the harness: vulnerable attacker delta +50000000000000000000 wei, patched half reverts with "value exceeds 128 bits".

pairs.vulnerability_class: Signature replay: the signed digest carries no nonce and the consumed-digest bookkeeping is never enforced, so one operator signature can be redeemed an unbounded number of times.
pairs.the_fix: One line added in redeem(): `require(!redeemed[dig], "voucher already redeemed");` immediately before the pre-existing `redeemed[dig] = true;` write, turning the dead bookkeeping flag into an enforced single-use check.
pairs.deploy_code: RebateTreasury target = new RebateTreasury{value: 100 ether}(0xe05fcC23807536bEe418f142D19fa0d21BB0cfF7);
pairs.why_patched_resists: The added `require(!redeemed[dig], "voucher already redeemed")` in redeem() consumes the digest on first redemption. The attacker's first `treasury.redeem(id)` still succeeds (so the contract is not bricked for honest relayers), but the second call recomputes the identical nonce-free digest, finds redeemed[dig] == true, and reverts; because attack() makes the three calls unconditionally with no try/catch, the whole transaction rolls back and the attacker's balance is unchanged. Verified: vulnerable half PASS (attacker 10 -> 10.75 ether, three relay fees plus a triple-drained 5 ether voucher), patched half FAIL with revert reason "voucher already redeemed".

pairs.vulnerability_class: Signature verification accepts ecrecover() returning address(0) for a malformed signature, matching the default-zero sessionKey of any account that never delegated.
pairs.the_fix: The authorization check in withdrawWithSession() changed from `require(recovered == sessionKey[account], "not authorized")` to `require(recovered != address(0) && recovered == sessionKey[account], "not authorized")`.
pairs.deploy_code:
DelegatedVault target = new DelegatedVault();
        target.depositFor{value: 60 ether}(address(uint160(0xC0FFEE)));
pairs.why_patched_resists: The attacker supplies v=27, r=0, s=0, for which the ecrecover precompile returns address(0) rather than reverting. The victim 0xC0FFEE never called setSessionKey, so sessionKey[VICTIM] is the default address(0) and the vulnerable equality check passes, letting the attacker name itself as `to` and take the whole 60 ether balance. The added `recovered != address(0) &&` conjunct in the patched half short-circuits on that exact case, so the same call reverts with "not authorized" before any balance is touched; a genuine delegated session key (a nonzero address) still passes both conjuncts, so honest delegation keeps working. Verified: vulnerable half PASS (attacker 10 -> 70 ether), patched half FAIL with revert reason "not authorized".

pairs.vulnerability_class: Front-runnable reveal: the commit-reveal window is not enforced, so an observer of a pending reveal can commit and claim in the same block ahead of the honest solver.
pairs.the_fix: One line added in claim(): `require(block.number >= claimableAt(msg.sender), "commitment too young");`, which finally enforces the MIN_COMMIT_AGE delay that the already-present claimableAt() helper and commitBlock mapping were computing but never checking.
pairs.why_patched_resists: deploy_code models the honest solver: it commits first and its reveal is still pending, which is how the attacker learns SECRET from the mempool. In the vulnerable half attack() commits and claims inside one transaction, so the commitment has age zero and the 25 ether is paid to the front-runner. The added `require(block.number >= claimableAt(msg.sender))` makes claimableAt(attacker) equal commitBlock+1 == block.number+1, so the same-transaction claim reverts with "commitment too young" and the attacker can never race a reveal it just observed. Separately verified that the patched contract is not bricked: a solver that commits, waits one block (vm.roll), then claims still receives the full 25 ether. Verified: vulnerable half PASS (attacker 10 -> 35 ether), patched half FAIL with revert reason "commitment too young".

pairs.vulnerability_class: Weak randomness: the payout seed is derived from block.timestamp and a blockhash that is fully known (zero) at settlement time, letting a bettor compute the winning side before staking.
pairs.the_fix: One line added in settle(): `require(block.number > b.placedAt, "round still open");`, forcing the seed's blockhash(b.placedAt) to be a real, not-yet-mined block hash at the time the side is chosen.
pairs.deploy_code: FlipCasino target = new FlipCasino{value: 80 ether}();
pairs.why_patched_resists: In the vulnerable half the attacker settles in the same block it bets, so b.placedAt == block.number and blockhash(b.placedAt) evaluates to zero; the entire seed reduces to keccak256(bytes32(0), block.timestamp, address(this)), which the attacker recomputes locally before calling placeBet and uses to pick the winning side, collecting a 10 ether pot on a 5 ether stake. The added `require(block.number > b.placedAt, "round still open")` rejects same-block settlement outright, so the attacker's single transaction reverts and its balance is unchanged; a bettor who waits is scored against blockhash(b.placedAt), a value that did not exist when the side was locked in, so the precomputation is useless. Separately verified that the patched contract is not bricked: a player who bets, advances one block (vm.roll), then settles is paid or loses normally. Verified: vulnerable half PASS (attacker 10 -> 15 ether), patched half FAIL with revert reason "round still open".
